reading.body:
CyrusOne's Sterling campus declares 116 megawatts of IT capacity across three buildings, the second-largest published power budget in Virginia and one of only 25 state facilities that disclose a figure at all.

Virginia has 330 mapped data center facilities. Just 25 of them publish IT capacity, totaling 1,603 megawatts. Sterling alone accounts for 7.2 percent of that declared total, concentrated in a single campus of three buildings with 1.18 million square feet of technical space. The disclosure rate, not the capacity, is the finding: for roughly 92 percent of Virginia's mapped facilities, power budget cannot be read and can only be inferred.

That matters because power budget is what sets the ceiling on accelerators a site can hold. At a stated assumption of 40 kilowatts per rack, Sterling's 116 megawatts would support roughly 2,900 racks, but that is arithmetic on an assumed density, not a measurement. A state where most facilities publish nothing leaves the actual scale of AI compute in Northern Virginia unknown, even as the region is treated as the country's densest concentration of data center capacity.

What the published specifications do not cover is substantial. They give no total power draw, no PUE, no cooling technology, no grid interconnection details, no tenant equipment, no utilization, and no stated constraints on expansion. The 116 megawatts is a nameplate figure for the campus, not a record of what it consumes. Nothing in the data says whether power supply or grid availability in Northern Virginia currently limits this site, and no certifications are listed for it.
